title: Nutrition and Mental Health: What We Know—and What We Don’t
description: Nutrition is not a cure for psychiatric disorders, but regular nourishment, protein, fiber-rich foods, hydration, and medication-specific food considerations can affect energy, concentration, physical health, and treatment tolerability. Evidence for supplements and “gut-brain” products varies.
body:
## Your Brain Needs Fuel Too

Nutrition and mental health are connected—but that doesn\'t mean there\'s a perfect \"mental health diet\.\"

Food isn\'t a cure for depression\, ADHD\, anxiety\, or addiction\, and you don\'t need to eat perfectly for treatment to work\.

What you eat and drink can\, however\, affect\:

## Energy • Concentration • Mood • Sleep • Medication Tolerance • Physical Health

At Ischys\, we\'re interested in patterns—not perfection\.

## Start With the Basics

Before worrying about the newest supplement or superfood\, ask\:

Am I eating regularly\?

Am I getting enough protein and nutrient\-dense foods\?

Am I drinking enough fluid\?

Am I going most of the day without eating and then crashing later\?

Sometimes the basics tell us more than we expect\.

## Your Brain Doesn\'t Like Running on Empty

Going long periods without eating can leave some people feeling\:

Tired

Irritable

Shaky

Headachy

Unfocused

Anxious

Mentally foggy

Those sensations can sometimes be confused with psychiatric symptoms or medication side effects\.

This doesn\'t mean everyone needs to eat on exactly the same schedule\.

It means notice how your body responds to yours\.

## Protein Matters

Protein provides amino acids that your body uses for many functions\, including making signaling molecules used throughout the brain and body\.

Rather than worrying about calculating the perfect number of grams\, consider whether you\'re regularly including foods such as\:

## Eggs • Fish • Poultry • Meat • Dairy • Beans • Lentils • Tofu • Nuts • Seeds

If you take medication that decreases your appetite\, eating something nutritious before your appetite disappears may be easier than trying to eat later\.

## Plants Bring More Than Vitamins

Fruits\, vegetables\, beans\, whole grains\, nuts\, and seeds provide combinations of\:

## Fiber • Vitamins • Minerals • Phytonutrients

Fiber also helps support the microorganisms living in the gastrointestinal tract—your gut microbiome\.

Researchers are actively studying the relationship between the gut microbiome and mental health\. The science is promising\, but we\'re still learning exactly how much changing the microbiome can improve specific psychiatric conditions\.

So rather than chasing expensive \"gut\-brain\" products\:

Start with food\.

## Omega\-3 Fatty Acids

Omega\-3 fatty acids—particularly EPA and DHA—are important components of cell membranes and have been studied extensively in brain and cardiovascular health\.

Food sources include fatty fish such as\:

## Salmon • Sardines • Trout • Herring

Omega\-3 supplements have also been studied for some psychiatric conditions\, but supplement formulations and evidence vary\.

\"Natural\" doesn\'t automatically mean appropriate for everyone\.

Talk with your healthcare provider before adding supplements\, particularly if you take medications or have medical conditions\.

## Hydration Counts

Even mild dehydration can make some people feel\:

tired • headachy • dizzy • irritable • less focused

Water needs vary based on body size\, activity\, climate\, pregnancy\, medical conditions\, medications\, and other factors\.

Instead of forcing yourself to hit an arbitrary number\:

Notice your pattern\.

If you\'ve had three coffees and an energy drink but almost no water today\, that\'s useful information\.

## ADHD \& Eating

ADHD can interfere with nutrition in several ways\.

You may\:

Forget to eat\.

Hyperfocus through meals\.

Choose whatever requires the least preparation\.

Seek highly rewarding foods when understimulated\.

And some ADHD medications can reduce appetite\.

If this sounds familiar\, don\'t rely entirely on remembering to eat\.

Try external supports\:

alarms • prepared snacks • visible food • simple meals • eating before medication suppresses

appetite

Making healthy choices easier often works better than relying on willpower\.

## Depression \& Food

When you\'re depressed\, cooking can feel like an enormous task\.

A nutritionally perfect meal that you don\'t have the energy to prepare isn\'t very helpful\.

Sometimes the better question is\:

\"What\'s the easiest reasonably nourishing thing I can eat\?\"

A sandwich\.

Yogurt and fruit\.

Eggs and toast\.

Soup\.

A smoothie\.

A simple frozen meal with something added to it\.

Fed is better than perfect\.

## Recovery \& Nutrition

Substance use can disrupt appetite\, eating patterns\, sleep\, gastrointestinal health\, and overall nutrition\.

During recovery\, hunger and cravings can also change\.

Re\-establishing regular meals can become part of rebuilding daily structure\.

Nutrition doesn\'t replace treatment for substance use disorders—but physical recovery and mental recovery aren\'t completely separate processes\.

## Food \& Your Medication

Some psychiatric medications can affect\:

Appetite • Weight • Blood sugar • Cholesterol • Nausea • Constipation • Dry mouth

Others may need to be taken with food\, while certain medications have specific food or supplement interactions\.

That\'s why we want to know about\:

Prescription medications \+ over\-the\-counter medications \+ vitamins \+ supplements \+ herbs \+ energy\/pre\-workout products

Bring us the whole list\.

## Supplements\: More Isn\'t Always Better

Supplements can be useful in selected situations\.

But supplements can also\:

Interact with medications

Cause side effects

Contain inconsistent amounts of active ingredients

Duplicate nutrients you\'re already taking

Be inappropriate for certain medical conditions

And sometimes a deficiency should be measured rather than guessed\.

At Ischys\, our goal is to use integrative approaches thoughtfully—not simply add more products\.

## Your Food \& Hydration Check\-In

Most days I\:

Eat fairly regularly

Frequently skip meals

Forget to eat

Have very little appetite

Eat mostly late in the day

Eat when stressed or emotional

Have strong food cravings

Have difficulty planning\/preparing food

Feel unsure about my nutrition

I regularly include\:

Protein

Fruits\/vegetables

Fiber\-rich foods

Omega\-3\-rich foods

Water\/other hydrating fluids

Something that makes eating well difficult for me\:

## Choose One Experiment

Not a diet\.

Not an overhaul\.

One experiment\.

I could try\:

Eating something with protein in the morning

Bringing a snack so I don\'t go all day without eating

Drinking more water

Adding one fruit or vegetable

Preparing one easy meal ahead of time

Setting an eating reminder

Eating before my medication reduces my appetite

## The Ischys Takeaway

You don\'t need a perfect diet\.

Before we chase complicated solutions\, let\'s make sure your brain and body are getting the basics\:

Regular fuel • Protein • Nutrient\-dense foods • Fiber • Hydration

Then we can individualize from there\.

## Notice Understand Experiment Track Discuss → → → →

This information is for general education and does not replace individualized medical or nutritional advice\. Dietary needs can differ substantially with medical conditions\, pregnancy\, eating disorders\, allergies\, medications\, and other individual circumstances\.
